title: Global Trends in Coupling and Birth Rates

Now there's constant entertainment on demand, whatever you want, whenever you want. And so that can offer and out-compete the guys next door, so people socialize less.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Speaker 2
dialogue_entries.text: Right, so these are quite interesting theories about why this is happening. We'll come back to some of them in a moment and link them possibly to other kind of cultural changes which you've hinted at. But John, just going back to the coupling, are there any places that are bucking the trend, which might give us some clues?

dialogue_entries.speaker: John
dialogue_entries.text: South Asia, so India, Pakistan, are certainly interesting in terms of having sustained quite high coupling rates there. Japan is interesting in the sense that it went through the latest stage of its demographic transition relatively early. So Japan's birth rate fell to very low levels earlier than many other countries. That's why we've been talking about it as the sort of poster child of falling birth rates for a long time. And that happened not completely independently of the decline of coupling, but in a kind of separate timing. So Japanese coupling rates are still falling today, even though its birth rate is relatively stable. So I would say in many countries, we've seen coupling and birth rates move in tandem, certainly in a lot of the notable ones, whether that's South Korea, we see the US, Finland. But there are some exceptions where those two things have happened at slightly different times.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Speaker 2
dialogue_entries.text: Let's talk about the aspects of an explanation for this, which most people immediately gravitate to, which are there are economic explanations for this. So John, let's talk about the one which I hear most at the moment, which is coupling is not happening because people can't afford to move in together because of the housing situation, a very kind of London eccentric view.

dialogue_entries.speaker: John
dialogue_entries.text: Yeah, this one's interesting because again, the picture looks really quite different in different countries. So for people in London, people in the UK, many parts of the US, This is both sort of measurably true and feels very obvious, that getting secure long-term housing, which in many anglophone countries essentially means owning your home, that has become harder to do. And of course, if you can't move out of your parents' home, then you're obviously not thinking about long-term relationships. Everything's a bit cramped. You don't really like the idea of you and your partner creeping around the house while your mum and dad are there as well. So that certainly feels like a plausible explanation for part of what we're seeing in the UK. But then a country like Finland has a very different thing going on, which is where a bit like Sweden, as Alice was mentioning, you have a high and rising share of young adults living on their own. Now, economically, that wouldn't make sense if the economics would encourage people to couple up, because then two incomes, easy to afford housing. But in Finland, there are actually policies which encourage that. They make it easier for solo young adults to get their own housing. So you can see how the economics and the policies can actually point in opposite directions and still produce that outcome. Now, I think that's interesting and worth remarking upon. But the fact that we see these similar trends in countries that have very different housing and economic situations, again, would at least suggest that a significant part of this trend is driven by the other stuff.

dialogue_entries.speaker: Speaker 2
dialogue_entries.text: Alice, how do you see this housing stroke cost of living argument as being the main driver? What are the problems with that?

dialogue_entries.speaker: Speaker 1
dialogue_entries.text: Well, I think, for example, look at Singapore. In Singapore, over 80% of housing is government owned, but it's got very low coupling. So I don't think that economics can explain. Moreover, as any of us know, that it's much cheaper to have a roommate to live together, right? You save costs on rent if two people are living together. So that can't be a full explanation for me. And especially why coupling is falling at very different levels of economic development across both towns and cities with different house to earn.
